text: So, I wrote a book and there's lots of stuff in that book and it was a huge effort for
me anyway to write it and now I think what I need to do is go back over it and maybe
read some bits out and explain what is in those bits and maybe try and encourage some
people to buy it. That would be great wouldn't it? And yeah, it's a foggy day here in London
Town and that's what I'm thinking about. Especially one of the things I'm thinking about is that
there was an idea that I realized was the kind of idea behind what I was writing but I never
kind of made it explicit which is that projects start out as being kind of essentially arguments
over to-do lists and how much it's going to cost for the to-do list. But if they stay there then
the whole thing goes a bit sterile and it doesn't really go where it needs to go. And what changes
everything is if you can connect to something valuable. So, this is why working software is
an extremely good idea. And if you can guess when it works you can get people to interact with it
or when you interact with it you start to understand what its real value is. And I was
so tied up with the idea of like seeing things from different points of view which is like one
of the values I would say of the book, one of the reasons it's valuable, we're talking about value
again, that I didn't make this explicit as a kind of single idea. But I think it's there, it's just
it's something that kind of very curiously people don't talk about that often. And also it's
how do I put this, it's kind of it's not mentioned when people are doing projects they don't talk
about how valuable it might be. I mean part of the reason for that is they don't really know,
they don't really know how it's going to be received and whether people are going to like
it or not. And they're kind of frightened of that. But that's why we're there, isn't it?
That's the whole reason for doing the thing.
